title: Spring's longing
hookLine: in the spring months the bride hears the koel and longs for the Beloved (Tukhari Barah Maha)

lines: A BIRD IN THE MANGO TREE.
cards: A bird calls from a mango tree, early, before the house is awake. Then again, a little farther off. The poem names it: the koel, singing in the mango tree.
Guru Nanak puts it right at the start of his year. The month is Chet, spring, and everything is beautiful. That's the trouble.
When the whole world is in bloom, the one thing missing is easier to hear.

teach.h: CHET: THE KOEL IN THE MANGO TREE.
teach.b: Here's Chet, in plain English, not word for word. Chet is good, spring is lovely, the bumblebees are beautiful, the forest is in flower.
Then the koel sings sweetly in the mango tree, and the bride asks: how can I bear this pain inside me? The bumblebee circles the flowering branch, and she says, how can I live, mother? I'm dying.
Notice: the poem doesn't call spring bad. It calls it lovely.
But when the one you love is far away, beauty can hurt more than gray skies. Every lovely thing points at who isn't there to see it.
Then Vaisakh, and the trees join in: Vaisakh is good, and the branches put on new clothes, fresh leaves like an outfit for a wedding.
And the bride stands looking at the door. Come home, Beloved, have mercy. Carry me across this hard ocean.

Without You, I'm not worth half a shell. In Sikh reading, the bride is the soul and the Beloved is God. So spring is the moment life is fullest around you, and something in you still says: not yet, not without You.
The poem doesn't shush that. It treats the ache as part of love, the sign she hasn't forgotten who she's waiting for.
That's today's line: the bird calls.

how: Sikhs sing Guru Nanak's Barah Maha in kirtan and read it as part of the Guru Granth Sahib, hearing the bride's longing in each month as the soul's longing for God.

o: a farmer's worry that the spring rains won't come
the ache of missing someone while everything blooms
the joy of spring festivals after a long winter

games.q: who's in the spring stanzas — tap the pairs.

s: in the poem, spring is called a bad time
Chet and Vaisakh are called good, even lovely. the beauty is what makes the absence hurt.
the bride says that without the Beloved she isn't worth half a shell
that's her cry in Vaisakh, as she asks Him to come home.
the poem tells the bride to stop longing
it lets the bird keep calling; the ache is treated as part of love.

games.q: it's Vaisakh. the trees are in fresh leaf and everything is lovely. what does the bride do?
o: go out and enjoy the season.
stand watching the door and ask the Beloved to come home.
forget the Beloved for a while.
games.why: she watches the door: come home, have mercy, carry me across. without You I'm not worth half a shell.

practice: Open a window or step outside if you can, or just listen to the room, and wait for a bird, any bird, near or far.
If one calls, follow the sound until it fades; if none comes, notice the waiting itself, the leaning-in, the small hope, the bride at the door. If you pray, say Waheguru softly between the calls.

wordCard.voice: Spring's longing. In Guru Nanak's Chet and Vaisakh, the koel sings and the trees put on new clothes, and all that beauty makes the absent Beloved felt more. Today's word.

orig.note: kokil: the koel, the bird that sings in the mango tree in Nanak's Chet.

carryVoice: Your line: the bird calls. Spring is lovely, and still the bride watches the door. That's today, done.
